title: Tips to combat lower back pain #1
summary: NH argues lower back pain usually comes from poor form (spinal rounding on deadlifts, rows, squats), so lower the weight and keep a neutral spine. He then recommends isolating the lower back with progressively loaded hyperextensions and reverse hypers, training abs with leg raises instead of crunches, and keeping good posture in daily life.

claims.claim: Lower back pain is usually the result of poor form that puts too much stress on the lumbar spine and SI joint.
The common culprits for lower back pain are deadlifts, rows and squats done with a rounded lumbar spine, which creates shear force and tissue inflammation.
Training-related back or tendon pain is often felt most the next morning because blood leaves the muscles and joints overnight, so the irritation is no longer masked.
If you're in pain, stop focusing on the weight: lower it, focus on form, and aim for sessions after which you wake up without pain.
A neutral spine is not a vertical torso: the torso can be angled (even parallel to the floor in Pendlay rows) as long as the spine is straight.
The more forward torso angle a lift has, the more potential there is for spinal rounding.
Before any pull or squat: bring the shoulders back, take a deep breath and brace the core, flex the upper back, and keep the spine position unchanged through the rep.
Rounding the back as the weight descends on rows, the 'good morning squat', or rounding the instant you pull a deadlift off the floor are all bad form and the source of pain.
Deadlifts alone are not enough for the lower back; like the core, it needs to be isolated.
Back hyperextensions are the best lower-back isolation: progress from bodyweight to plates, dumbbells, then a barbell to make the lower back 'bulletproof'.
Hyperextensions train the lower back, hamstrings and glutes while stressing the muscles without stressing the spine.
Reverse hypers are another good lower-back exercise if your gym has one.
Train abs more, but avoid crunches, which compromise the lower back by rounding at the top; do leg raises on the floor or from a bar with a straight body instead.
Posture in daily life matters: sit and walk with a straight spine and head; slouching damages the lower back long term.
In an office chair, put a pillow behind your lower back to create curvature and force an upright posture.

exercises.name: Back hyperextension
exercises.why: isolates lower back, hamstrings, glutes without stressing the spine

exercises.name: Leg raises (floor or hanging)
cues: keep the body straight, don't curl up
exercises.why: core work without the lumbar rounding of crunches

exercises.name: Crunches
exercises.why: criticised: round the lower back at the top

exercises.name: Pendlay row
cues: torso parallel to the floor but spine neutral
exercises.why: example of neutral spine at an angle
